content.content:
## West Africa -- English on a continent of many voices

When you think of the English-speaking world, you might picture Britain, the USA or Australia. But some of the largest English-speaking countries are in **West Africa**. Here, English is not usually people's mother tongue -- it is an *official language* (offisielt språk) they share on top of hundreds of local languages.

In this chapter you will explore two important West African nations:

- **Nigeria** -- Africa's most populous country, home to Nollywood films, Afrobeats music and world-famous authors
- **Ghana** -- the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to win independence from Britain

You will also learn about **Nigerian Pidgin**, a lively everyday language, and think about *why* English is spoken so widely in this part of the world.

## Nigeria -- Africa's giant

**Facts about Nigeria:**
- Population: about 220 million -- the most populous country in Africa and the sixth most populous in the world
- Capital: Abuja. Largest city: Lagos, a huge, fast-growing megacity
- Official language: English
- More than 500 local languages are spoken. The three largest ethnic and language groups are the **Hausa**, the **Yoruba** and the **Igbo**
- Former British colony -- independence in 1960

**Why English?**
Because Nigeria has so many languages, no single local language is spoken by everyone. English -- left behind by British colonial rule -- became the country's **lingua franca** (fellesspråk that people with different mother tongues use to understand each other). It is used in schools, government, business and the media.

**A young country:** More than half of Nigerians are under the age of 19. This young population drives a booming culture of music, film and technology that reaches the whole world.

content.title: Nigerian Pidgin English
content.content:
**Nigerian Pidgin** (also called *Naija*) is an everyday language spoken by tens of millions of Nigerians. Like Jamaican Patois, it grew out of contact between English and local African languages, and it now has its own grammar and vocabulary.

Many Nigerians switch between Standard English (in school and formal situations) and Pidgin (with friends and family) -- a bit like switching between bokmål and dialect.

**Examples of Nigerian Pidgin:**

| Pidgin | English |
|---|---|
| *How far?* | How are you? / What's up? |
| *Wetin dey happen?* | What's going on? |
| *I dey come* | I'm coming |
| *No wahala* | No problem |
| *Chop* | Eat / food |
| *Sabi* | To know / understand |
| *Abi?* | Right? / Isn't it? |
| *Comot* | Go away / get out |

**Is it 'bad English'?** No. Linguists see Pidgin as a real language with its own rules. The BBC even has a news service called *BBC News Pidgin*, written entirely in Nigerian Pidgin, read by millions of people across West Africa.

## Nigerian culture -- film, music and literature

### Nollywood
Nigeria's film industry is nicknamed **Nollywood** (from *Nigeria* + *Hollywood*). It is one of the largest film industries in the world by number of films made each year -- ahead of Hollywood in output. Nollywood films are usually made quickly and cheaply, and they are hugely popular across Africa and among African communities worldwide.

### Afrobeats
**Afrobeats** (not to be confused with the older *Afrobeat* of Fela Kuti) is a modern pop style that mixes West African rhythms with hip-hop, R&B and dancehall. Nigerian stars like **Burna Boy**, **Wizkid** and **Tiwa Savage** now fill stadiums in Europe and America. Afrobeats is one of the ways young Nigerians share their culture with the world.

### World-class literature
Nigeria has produced some of the most celebrated writers in the English language:
- **Chinua Achebe** wrote *Things Fall Apart* (1958), one of the most widely read African novels ever. It tells the story of an Igbo community as British colonisers arrive.
- **Wole Soyinka** became the first African to win the Nobel Prize in Literature (1986).
- **Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie** is a leading writer today. Her famous talk *"The Danger of a Single Story"* warns that if we hear only one type of story about a place or people, we end up with a false, narrow picture of them.

These writers use English -- the coloniser's language -- to tell African stories on their own terms.

content.content:
## Ghana -- the pride of Africa

**Facts about Ghana:**
- Population: about 33 million
- Capital: Accra
- Official language: English
- Main local languages include **Twi** (part of the Akan group), Ewe and Ga
- Former British colony known as the *Gold Coast*

### A proud history
In **1957, Ghana became the first country in sub-Saharan Africa to gain independence from European colonial rule**. Its first leader, **Kwame Nkrumah**, became a symbol of African freedom and inspired independence movements across the whole continent. Ghana's flag has a black star that stands for African freedom and unity.

### Ghanaian culture
- **Kente cloth:** a brightly coloured, hand-woven fabric with patterns that carry meanings. Once worn by royalty, it is now a symbol of African identity around the world.
- **Highlife and Azonto:** Highlife is a joyful dance music that mixes local rhythms with guitars and brass. *Azonto* is a popular dance and music style loved by young Ghanaians.
- **Respect and community:** Ghanaian culture places great value on greetings, respect for elders and a strong sense of community.

Like Nigerians, most Ghanaians grow up speaking a local language at home and learn English at school, so many people are comfortable in two, three or more languages.

content.title: English as a post-colonial language
content.content:
**Colonialism** is when one country takes control of another and rules its land and people. Britain colonised much of West Africa and made English the language of government and schools. When these countries became independent, they kept English -- but why?

**Reasons countries kept English:**
- It is a **neutral** choice: picking one local language over the others could cause conflict between ethnic groups.
- It connects them to the wider world of trade, science and diplomacy.
- It already had a place in schools, courts and government.

**But there are challenges (utfordringer) too:**
- Children who don't speak English at home can struggle in school.
- Some local languages lose speakers and risk dying out.
- Using the former coloniser's language can feel like a painful reminder of the past.

Writers like Chinua Achebe chose to write in English so their stories could reach the world, while filling that English with African words, proverbs and rhythms. In this way, West Africans have made English **their own**.

## West African English -- a variety of its own

West African English is not one single accent, but there are some shared features across Nigeria, Ghana and neighbouring countries.

**Pronunciation:**
- The *th* sounds are often replaced: *think* -> *tink*, *that* -> *dat*
- Speech often has a clear, syllable-timed rhythm, different from British or American English

**Vocabulary and loanwords:**
- *Danfo* -- a yellow minibus used for public transport in Lagos
- *Okada* -- a motorcycle taxi
- *Chop* -- to eat (also used in Pidgin)
- *Wahala* -- trouble or problem

**Local flavour in everyday English:**
- Proverbs are highly valued: 'Until the lion learns to write, every story will glorify the hunter.'
- Greetings are longer and more important than in Norway -- asking about someone's family and health is polite and expected.

These features show, once again, that there is no single 'correct' English. English changes and grows wherever it is spoken.

content.content:
## Oppsummering

**Nigeria:**
- Afrikas mest folkerike land (~220 millioner), over 500 språk
- Engelsk som lingua franca; nigeriansk Pidgin i dagliglivet
- Nollywood-film, Afrobeats-musikk og verdenskjente forfattere (Achebe, Soyinka, Adichie)

**Ghana:**
- Første land sør for Sahara som ble selvstendig (1957), Kwame Nkrumah
- Engelsk som offisielt språk; lokale språk som Twi
- Kente-stoff, highlife- og azonto-musikk, sterk fellesskapskultur

**Engelsk som post-kolonialt språk:**
- Beholdt fordi det er 'nøytralt' mellom mange folkegrupper og kobler landet til verden
- Utfordringer: barn uten engelsk hjemme, og lokale språk som trues
- Vestafrikanere har gjort engelsk til 'sitt eget' -- fylt med egne ord, ordtak og rytmer

Vest-Afrika viser at engelsk ikke tilhører ett folk eller ett land -- det lever, endrer seg og bærer mange kulturer.
